title: Histology of the Lymphoid Organs
subject: Immune System (IMMU)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the lymph node, spleen, thymus, and mucosa associated lymphoid tissue are built, and why each layout suits its job. Secondary lymphoid organs place antigen, antigen-presenting cells, T cells, and B cells in separate zones that are wired together, so rare lymphocytes can find their antigen and their helpers. The thymus is built for selection rather than filtering. Board questions show a section or describe a patient and ask which zone holds which cell, which zone is empty in an immunodeficiency, which zone enlarges in a reactive node, how blood moves through the spleen, or how mucosal IgA is made.
prerequisites: Lymphocyte lineages and markers: B cells (CD19, CD20), helper T cells (CD4), cytotoxic T cells (CD8)
MHC class I and class II and how dendritic cells present antigen
Antibody isotypes, class switching, and plasma cell differentiation
Basic connective tissue: reticular fibers (type III collagen) and endothelium
Pharyngeal pouch derivatives and the anatomy of the ileum and pharynx

connections.to: Cells and development of the immune system (IM-1)
connections.how: The lineages made in bone marrow and thymus are the cells that fill each zone described here.
Which zone is empty on a node or spleen biopsy tells you whether the T cell or B cell lineage has failed.
The red pulp removes old, rigid, and inclusion-bearing red cells, which explains extravascular hemolysis, splenomegaly, and postsplenectomy blood smear changes.
Peyer patches and M cells are the entry point for Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia and the source of intestinal secretory IgA.
Reactive follicles must be told apart from follicular lymphoma, and chronic mucosal inflammation can give rise to MALT lymphoma.

terms.def: An organ (lymph node, spleen, MALT) where mature naive lymphocytes meet antigen and start adaptive responses, as opposed to the primary organs (bone marrow, thymus) where lymphocytes develop.
A round cluster of resting naive B cells on a mesh of follicular dendritic cells, without a germinal center.
The pale center of a secondary follicle where antigen-activated B cells proliferate, undergo somatic hypermutation and class switching, and are selected for high affinity.
A stromal (non-bone marrow) cell of follicles that holds intact antigen as immune complexes on complement and Fc receptors for B cells to sample.
A postcapillary venule with plump cuboidal endothelium, found in the T cell zones of nodes and MALT, through which naive lymphocytes leave the blood.
The cuff of T cells that surrounds the central arteriole in splenic white pulp.
The region surrounding splenic white pulp where incoming blood meets macrophages and marginal zone B cells that respond rapidly to blood-borne antigens.
The splenic cords of the red pulp: a spongy mesh of reticular cells and macrophages lying between venous sinusoids.
A thymic epithelial cell that forms the meshwork supporting thymocytes, contributes to the blood thymus barrier, and presents self MHC during selection.
A concentric whorl of flattened, partly keratinized epithelial reticular cells found only in the thymic medulla.
A specialized cell of the follicle-associated epithelium over MALT that transports luminal antigen by transcytosis to immune cells beneath it.
Dimeric IgA joined by a J chain and carrying secretory component, the main antibody released onto mucosal surfaces.

blocks.text: A lymph node is a bean-shaped filter placed along lymphatic vessels. Its job is to bring antigen arriving in lymph together with the few naive lymphocytes that can recognize it. A dense connective tissue capsule surrounds the node and sends trabeculae inward, and a meshwork of reticular fibers (type III collagen) made by fibroblastic reticular cells supports the rest. Several afferent lymphatics, which carry valves, pierce the convex surface; one or two efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum, where the artery enters and the vein exits.

blocks.title: Path of lymph through a node
steps: Afferent lymphatics pierce the capsule
Subcapsular (marginal) sinus under the capsule
Trabecular (cortical) sinuses along trabeculae
Medullary sinuses between medullary cords
Efferent lymphatic leaves at the hilum
blocks.caption: Sinuses are lined by endothelium and crossed by reticular fibers, which slow lymph and expose it to macrophages and dendritic cells.

blocks.text: Antigen is captured along this path. Macrophages lining the subcapsular sinus trap particles and pass intact antigen to B cells in the follicles below, while small soluble antigens travel through narrow reticular fiber conduits into the cortex. Dendritic cells that picked up antigen in the tissue arrive in the same lymph already carrying processed peptide on MHC.
Cortex, paracortex, and medulla

The outer cortex holds the B cell follicles. A primary follicle is a dense, uniform cluster of resting naive B cells on a network of follicular dendritic cells. After antigen stimulation it becomes a secondary follicle, with a pale germinal center surrounded by a darker mantle zone of naive IgM and IgD positive B cells. The germinal center has a dark zone, where proliferating centroblasts undergo somatic hypermutation, and a light zone, where centrocytes compete for antigen held on follicular dendritic cells and for help from follicular helper T cells. Cells that fail selection die by apoptosis and are eaten by tingible body macrophages.

The paracortex (deep cortex) is the T cell zone, rich in CD4 and CD8 T cells and interdigitating dendritic cells. It contains the high endothelial venules, the gateway by which most naive lymphocytes enter the node. The medulla consists of medullary cords, which hold plasma cells, macrophages, and lymphocytes, alternating with medullary sinuses. Plasma cells formed in the cortex settle in the cords and release antibody into the efferent lymph.

blocks.caption: B cells occupy the outer cortex, T cells the deep cortex, and plasma cells the medulla.

blocks.text: The layout explains the timing of a response. Helper T cells activated in the paracortex move to the edge of the follicle, where B cells that have taken up the same antigen present it to them. This T cell and B cell meeting at the follicle border launches the germinal center reaction that produces high-affinity, class-switched antibody.

sections.title: Depleted and expanded zones in disease

blocks.text: Each zone of the node is filled by the lymphocytes that home to it, so a node biopsy works as a map of which lineage is present. If a lineage never develops, its zone stays empty while the other zones still form. If a lineage is stimulated strongly, its zone enlarges.
Depleted zones

DiGeorge syndrome is most often a 22q11.2 deletion that disrupts development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. The thymus (third pouch) is small or absent, so few mature T cells reach the periphery, and the paracortex and the splenic PALS are thin or empty. B cell follicles still form, but germinal centers may be small because B cells need T cell help to build them.

X-linked agammaglobulinemia is caused by a defect in Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK), a kinase needed for pre-B cell receptor signaling. B cell development stops at the pre-B stage in the marrow, so lymph nodes and spleen lack follicles, germinal centers, and plasma cells, and the tonsils are tiny or absent. The paracortex is normal because T cells are unaffected. Symptoms usually begin after about 6 months of age, once maternal IgG has been catabolized.
Expanded zones

Reactive follicular hyperplasia follows strong B cell stimulation. Follicles are numerous and large, with polarized germinal centers of varied size, many tingible body macrophages, and an intact mantle. Typical causes are rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis, syphilis, and early HIV infection. Reactive paracortical hyperplasia follows T cell stimulation, which expands the paracortex with activated T cells and large immunoblasts that can push follicles aside. Typical causes are viral infections such as infectious mononucleosis (EBV), recent vaccination, and drugs such as phenytoin.

blocks.title: Zone changes in lymph nodes
rows: Present; germinal centers may be small
BTK defect; arrest at pre-B stage
Neither functional T nor B cells
blocks.caption: Absence of a lineage empties its zone; stimulation of a lineage expands its zone.

blocks.text: Reactive follicles must be distinguished from follicular lymphoma, a neoplasm most often driven by t(14;18), which places BCL2 next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus. Neoplastic follicles are crowded back to back, uniform in size, lack polarity and tingible body macrophages (because BCL2 blocks apoptosis), and their germinal center cells stain for BCL2, whereas reactive germinal center cells do not.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading an empty zone
blocks.text: A 9-month-old boy has recurrent otitis media and pneumonia with Streptococcus pneumoniae. Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM are all very low, and the tonsils are barely visible. Which lymph node zone is depleted? Recurrent infection with encapsulated bacteria points to failure of antibody, not of T cells. Onset after 6 months fits loss of maternal IgG. Tiny tonsils mean lymphoid follicles are missing. Therefore the B cell zones (cortical follicles and germinal centers) and the medullary plasma cells are absent, while the paracortex is normal. This is the pattern of X-linked agammaglobulinemia. With hypocalcemia, a conotruncal heart defect, and viral or fungal infections instead, the paracortex would be empty (DiGeorge syndrome).

blocks.predict: A node from a child with complete DiGeorge syndrome has primary follicles but almost no germinal centers. Why are the follicles present but not active?
blocks.explain: B cells develop normally in the marrow and home to follicles using CXCL13, so primary follicles form. Germinal centers require CD40 ligand and cytokines from follicular helper T cells, which are missing, so B cells cannot be driven into the germinal center reaction.
blocks.check: The DiGeorge paragraph and the T cell and B cell meeting at the follicle border in C01.

blocks.text: The spleen is the largest secondary lymphoid organ and the only one placed in the bloodstream rather than in lymph. It has no afferent lymphatics, so its lymphoid tissue is arranged around arterioles instead of sinuses. A dense connective tissue capsule sends trabeculae inward carrying arteries and veins. The cut surface shows small gray-white nodules (white pulp) scattered in a dark red background (red pulp).
White pulp and marginal zone

White pulp forms around central arterioles. T cells form the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) that cuffs each arteriole, and B cell follicles, primary or with germinal centers, sit beside the sheath and push the arteriole to an eccentric position. Surrounding the white pulp is the marginal zone, where many arteriolar branches open. Blood here percolates past marginal zone macrophages and marginal zone B cells. These B cells respond quickly, often without T cell help, to polysaccharide capsules, producing IgM that opsonizes and activates complement.
Red pulp

Red pulp consists of splenic cords (cords of Billroth) and venous sinusoids. The cords are a spongy reticular mesh full of macrophages and blood cells. The sinusoids are lined by long, rod-shaped endothelial cells held by a basal lamina arranged in rings, like barrel staves and hoops, leaving narrow slits between the cells. To enter a sinusoid from a cord, a red cell about 7 to 8 micrometers across must fold and squeeze through a slit only a few micrometers wide, or less.

blocks.title: Blood flow through the spleen
steps: Splenic artery enters at the hilum
Trabecular arteries in connective tissue trabeculae
Central arteriole surrounded by PALS
Branches empty into the marginal zone
Penicillar arterioles, then sheathed capillaries
Open: into cords; closed: directly into sinusoids
Red cells squeeze through slits into sinusoids
Pulp veins, trabecular veins, splenic vein
blocks.caption: In humans most blood takes the open route through the cords, which is the route that tests red cell deformability. The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.

blocks.text: This design explains splenic function. Normal red cells, which live about 120 days, deform easily and pass. Aged cells, spherocytes, sickled cells, and antibody-coated cells are held in the cords and eaten by macrophages (culling), which is extravascular hemolysis. Rigid inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) and Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) are pinched out as the cell squeezes through (pitting). The spleen also holds about one third of circulating platelets.

blocks.title: Splenic compartments
rows: T cell activation by blood-borne antigen
B cells; germinal centers when active
Antibody responses with T cell help
Capture of blood-borne antigen; rapid IgM to encapsulated bacteria
Culling of old or rigid red cells; phagocytosis
Deformability test; return of blood to veins
blocks.caption: White pulp is immune; red pulp is a filter for blood cells.

blocks.title: Worked example: after splenectomy
blocks.text: A man has his spleen removed after trauma. Predict his smear and his infection risk. Without cords and slits, inclusions are no longer pitted, so Howell-Jolly bodies appear in red cells. Target cells and a rise in platelet count follow because cells are no longer remodeled or pooled in the spleen. Without the marginal zone, blood-borne encapsulated bacteria are neither trapped by macrophages nor met by rapid IgM, and opsonization is impaired. He is therefore at lifelong risk of overwhelming sepsis from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis.

The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ in the anterior superior mediastinum where T cells mature. Its framework is epithelial, derived from third pharyngeal pouch endoderm, and is colonized by T cell precursors from the bone marrow. Septa from a thin capsule divide each lobe into incomplete lobules. Each lobule has a dark outer cortex and a pale inner medulla, and the medulla is continuous from lobule to lobule.

The supporting cells are epithelial reticular cells (thymic epithelial cells), not fibroblasts and reticular fibers as in a node. Joined by desmosomes into a meshwork, they express MHC class I and II and secrete IL-7 and thymic hormones.
Cortex

The cortex stains dark because it is packed with small immature thymocytes, mostly CD4 and CD8 double positive cells. Cortical epithelial cells carry self MHC and test each new T cell receptor. Thymocytes that bind self MHC weakly receive a survival signal (positive selection), and the class they bind decides their fate: class II produces CD4 cells and class I produces CD8 cells. Most thymocytes fail and die by apoptosis, so macrophages with ingested debris are scattered through the cortex.

The blood thymus barrier protects cortical thymocytes from circulating antigen, so that selection is shaped by self antigens presented by thymic cells. It is present in the cortex only and has three layers: continuous capillary endothelium with tight junctions and a thick basal lamina, a perivascular space containing macrophages that remove escaping antigen, and a sheath of epithelial reticular cells with their own basal lamina.
Medulla

The medulla stains paler because its T cells are fewer, larger, and mostly mature single positive CD4 or CD8 cells. Here negative selection removes cells that bind self peptide on MHC strongly. Medullary epithelial cells use the transcription factor AIRE to express proteins normally made only in other organs, such as insulin, and dendritic cells present them as well; some self-reactive CD4 cells become regulatory T cells instead of dying. Hassall corpuscles, whorls of flattened, partly keratinized epithelial cells, are the medulla's signature and may support regulatory T cell development.

steps: Marrow precursors enter near the corticomedullary junction
Double negative cells move to the outer cortex
Double positive cells undergo positive selection in cortex
Survivors commit to CD4 or CD8
Negative selection in medulla using AIRE and dendritic cells
Mature naive T cells exit to the circulation
blocks.caption: Position in the lobule tracks maturity: immature in the outer cortex, mature in the medulla.

blocks.title: Telling cortex from medulla, and thymus from lymph node
rows: Follicles at periphery; pale germinal centers
No T cell selection; B cell selection in germinal centers
blocks.caption: A lobulated organ with dark cortex, pale medulla, Hassall corpuscles, and no follicles or sinuses is thymus.

blocks.text: The thymus involutes after puberty and is progressively replaced by adipose tissue, though adults still export some T cells. Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers in the thymic medulla are abnormal; this thymic follicular hyperplasia is classically associated with myasthenia gravis.

blocks.predict: If AIRE were absent but cortical selection were normal, would T cell numbers fall, and what disease pattern would follow?
blocks.explain: T cell numbers would be roughly normal because positive selection works. Cells reactive to tissue-restricted self proteins would escape negative selection, causing autoimmunity against several endocrine organs, the pattern of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1.
blocks.check: The cortex and medulla paragraphs on positive and negative selection.

sections.title: Mucosa associated lymphoid tissue and secretory IgA

blocks.text: Mucosa associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) is lymphoid tissue in the lamina propria and submucosa of the gastrointestinal, respiratory, and urogenital tracts. It ranges from scattered lymphocytes and plasma cells, through solitary follicles, to organized aggregates such as tonsils, Peyer patches, and the appendix. Gut-associated tissue is called GALT and bronchus-associated tissue BALT. MALT has no capsule and no afferent lymphatics. Instead of waiting for antigen to arrive in lymph, it samples antigen directly from the lumen through the overlying epithelium.

blocks.title: Tonsils and Peyer patches
rows: Deep branching crypts; partial capsule on the deep surface
Folds rather than deep crypts; on posterior nasopharynx wall
Posterior tongue; usually a single shallow crypt per unit
Simple columnar with M cells over domes
Ileum, antimesenteric wall; follicles extend into submucosa
blocks.caption: Each tonsil is identified by its covering epithelium and crypt pattern; Peyer patches are identified by ileal location and dome epithelium.

blocks.text: Peyer patches and M cells

Peyer patches are aggregates of lymphoid follicles with germinal centers in the ileal lamina propria and submucosa. Each follicle bulges toward the lumen as a dome covered by follicle-associated epithelium, which has few goblet cells (and so less mucus) and contains M cells (microfold cells). An M cell has short, irregular microfolds instead of a brush border, a thin glycocalyx, and a basolateral pocket holding lymphocytes and dendritic cells. It takes up luminal antigens and microbes by endocytosis and releases them intact into the pocket, a process called transcytosis. Dendritic cells in the dome then carry antigen to T cells in the interfollicular areas, which contain HEVs, and to B cells in the follicles. Some pathogens exploit this route, including Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, and poliovirus.
From M cell to secretory IgA

B cells activated in Peyer patches switch preferentially to IgA. TGF-beta from local cells is the main switch signal, supported by helper T cells and by T cell independent signals. Gut dendritic cells make retinoic acid, which gives the activated cells the gut-homing integrin alpha4beta7 and the chemokine receptor CCR9. The cells leave through lymph to the mesenteric nodes, enter the blood, and return by binding MAdCAM-1 on mucosal venules, settling as IgA plasma cells in the lamina propria. Some primed cells reach other mucosae and lactating breast, so mucosal immunity is partly shared.

blocks.title: Generation of secretory IgA
steps: M cell transcytoses luminal antigen
Dome dendritic cells present to T and B cells
TGF-beta drives class switch to IgA
Retinoic acid induces alpha4beta7 and CCR9
Cells return to lamina propria via MAdCAM-1
Plasma cell secretes dimeric IgA with J chain
Polymeric Ig receptor carries IgA across epithelium
Cleavage leaves secretory component on luminal IgA
blocks.caption: Secretory component shields IgA from proteases, so it remains intact in the gut lumen.

blocks.text: The plasma cell makes IgA as a dimer joined by a J chain. The polymeric Ig receptor on the basolateral surface of the epithelial cell binds the J chain-containing dimer, carries it across the cell in vesicles, and is cleaved at the apical surface. The fragment that stays bound is secretory component. Secretory IgA blocks microbial attachment and neutralizes toxins without activating the classical complement pathway, so it protects without inflaming the mucosa. More IgA is produced each day than any other isotype, mostly at mucosal surfaces. Chronic antigen stimulation can induce MALT in sites that normally lack it, such as the stomach in Helicobacter pylori gastritis, which is the setting for gastric MALT lymphoma.

integration.text: The four organs follow one principle: structure places antigen and the right lymphocytes in the same space. Nodes filter lymph through sinuses, the spleen filters blood through the marginal zone and red pulp, MALT samples the lumen through M cells, and the thymus excludes blood antigen behind a barrier so selection is made on self. Embryology explains DiGeorge syndrome (third and fourth pouches), and molecular immunology explains where cells settle: CCR7 ligands hold T cells in the paracortex, CXCL13 holds B cells in follicles, and alpha4beta7 with MAdCAM-1 returns IgA plasma cells to the gut.

Pathology reads these zones backward. An empty paracortex or PALS means T cell failure, absent follicles and tonsils mean B cell failure, and enlarged zones show which lineage is responding. Histologic patterns are a guide rather than proof: lineage defects are confirmed by flow cytometry, immunoglobulin levels, and genetic testing, and reactive hyperplasia is separated from lymphoma with immunostains such as BCL2.

summary: Lymph flows from afferent lymphatics through subcapsular, trabecular, and medullary sinuses to the efferent vessel at the hilum.
In a lymph node, B cells occupy outer cortical follicles, T cells the paracortex with its HEVs, and plasma cells the medullary cords.
Naive lymphocytes enter through HEVs using L-selectin, CCR7, and LFA-1; CXCL13 then draws B cells into follicles.
DiGeorge syndrome empties the paracortex and PALS; X-linked agammaglobulinemia removes follicles, germinal centers, plasma cells, and tonsils.
Follicular hyperplasia reflects B cell stimulation; paracortical hyperplasia reflects T cell stimulation such as EBV, vaccination, or phenytoin.
Splenic white pulp has T cells in the PALS, B cells in follicles, and a marginal zone that defends against encapsulated bacteria.
Splenic blood passes central arterioles, the marginal zone, and penicillar arterioles into cords, then squeezes through sinusoid slits into veins.
The red pulp culls rigid red cells and pits inclusions, so asplenia shows Howell-Jolly bodies and risk of sepsis from encapsulated organisms.
Thymic cortex is dark with immature thymocytes, positive selection, and the blood thymus barrier; medulla is pale with mature T cells, AIRE, and Hassall corpuscles.
M cells in Peyer patch domes transcytose antigen; TGF-beta drives IgA switching, and the polymeric Ig receptor delivers dimeric IgA with secretory component.

verify: The width of the interendothelial slits in splenic sinusoids is quoted variably (from under 1 micrometer to about 3 micrometers); this chapter states only that they are a few micrometers or less.
The fraction of thymocytes that die during selection is quoted from about 95% to over 98%; this chapter says most die without giving a figure.
The proportion of platelets held in the spleen is given as about one third in most texts; confirm the value NABNE expects.

Human splenic marginal zone anatomy differs from rodents (a perifollicular zone is described in humans), and the relative share of open versus closed circulation is debated; the chapter states that open circulation predominates in humans.

Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Billroth, Hassall, and Peyer, the term Schweigger-Seidel sheath, or the Ross classification of epithelial reticular cells (types I to VI), which are omitted here.
The role of Hassall corpuscles in regulatory T cell development (via TSLP-conditioned dendritic cells) comes from research literature and is stated cautiously.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: lymph-node-zones (capsule, sinuses, follicles, paracortex, medulla with afferent and efferent vessels), spleen-blood-path (central arteriole, PALS, marginal zone, cords, sinusoids), thymus-lobule (cortex, medulla, Hassall corpuscle, blood thymus barrier), and peyer-patch-dome (M cell with basolateral pocket over a follicle).
